ui.gs.title: Getting Started
ui.gs.description: How to install orn-ui and wrap your app in <UIProvider> — required before any component renders.
ui.gs.lede: Three steps: install, wrap your app in UIProvider, then import components. Skipping step 2 is the single most common way to break orn-ui — every hook and every component reads theme, icons and labels from it.
ui.gs.step1.title: 1. Install
ui.gs.step1.body: Either the whole package, or just the components you need via the CLI (no npm dependency for the second option — see each component page for its own command).
ui.gs.step2.title: 2. Wrap your app in UIProvider
ui.gs.step2.body: UIProvider is the single entry point of the library. It resolves the active theme (system or manual override) and injects icons, safe-area insets and default labels to the whole tree. Mount it once, above your navigator — root of App.tsx is the usual place.
ui.gs.step2.warning: Every orn-ui component and hook (useColors, useTheme, Button, Input, all of them) throws "this hook must be used within a <UIProvider>" if rendered outside one. There is no fallback and no silent default — it fails loudly at runtime, not at build time.
ui.gs.step3.title: 3. Use components
ui.gs.step3.body: Now every component page on this site works as shown — copy a variant snippet, it renders. See the component list below.
ui.gs.props.title: UIProvider props
ui.gs.requiresProviderNote: This component (like every orn-ui component) must render inside a <UIProvider> ancestor, or it throws at runtime.
ui.gs.safeArea.title: Recommended: SafeAreaUIProvider
ui.gs.safeArea.body: UIProvider defaults insets to {top:0,bottom:0,left:0,right:0} — harmless until you open a full-screen Modal (slides under the notch) or a BottomSheet (sits flush against the gesture bar). SafeAreaUIProvider is UIProvider with useSafeAreaInsets() already wired in — use it instead of UIProvider and this is handled.
ui.gs.safeArea.subpath: It lives in its own subpath (orn-ui/safe-area), on purpose: it is the only file in the library that imports a third-party package (react-native-safe-area-context). Nothing in the main orn-ui entry point references it, so a plain import { Button } from 'orn-ui' never pulls it in — the rest of the library stays zero-dependency.
ui.gs.safeArea.install: Needs react-native-safe-area-context as a peer (optional — only required if you use this import):
ui.gs.safeArea.nestedNote: Already mounting a <SafeAreaProvider> higher up (some React Navigation templates do)? Pass mountSafeAreaProvider={false} — a nested provider measures its own View's frame, not the window's, so insets read zero from inside it.
ui.gs.safeArea.propsNote: Plus every UIProvider prop above except insets (still accepted, but optional — it overrides the measured value instead of being required).
ui.typography.name: Typography
ui.typography.install.cli: Install the file (copies Title, Subtitle, Body and Caption together, no npm dependency)
ui.typography.install.package: Or install the whole package and import all four
ui.typography.description: Title, Subtitle, Body and Caption — the 4 text styles of orn-ui, one shared install.
ui.typography.lede: Four text styles, one file, one install. Title, Subtitle, Body and Caption all come from the same Text.tsx and ship together — installing one gets you all four.
ui.typography.cherryPick: Installing copies the whole file, but you only import and render what you actually use — you do not need all four.
ui.typography.sharedProps: Same props for Title, Subtitle, Body and Caption — all four share the same TypographyProps.
ui.typography.title.usage: Page and section headings — the largest, boldest style. One or two per screen, not more.
ui.typography.subtitle.usage: Secondary heading, right below a Title, or standalone for a lighter section header.
ui.typography.body.usage: The default paragraph style — most of the text on a screen should be Body.
ui.typography.caption.usage: Small print: secondary hints, metadata, timestamps, helper text under a field.
ui.ad.title: Atomic Design
ui.ad.description: What atomic design is, why orn-ui is built on it, and how to apply the same three layers to any frontend project.
ui.ad.lede: Atomic design organises an interface into a few layers that build on each other: small pieces combine into bigger ones, and nothing ever depends on something above it. orn-ui ships in those layers — and the same structure works in any frontend codebase, React Native or not.
ui.ad.why.title: Why orn-ui was built
ui.ad.why.body1: Most component libraries try to cover web and mobile from a single codebase. That reach has a price on a phone: extra abstraction layers, web-oriented dependencies riding along into the bundle, styling engines resolving at runtime. You pay for portability you are not using.
ui.ad.why.body2: orn-ui goes the other way. It is 100% React Native with zero runtime dependencies — react and react-native are the only peers. Nothing to compile, no styling engine to configure, no bundler plugin to add.
ui.ad.why.point1.title: Install a component, not a library
ui.ad.why.point1.body: npx orn-ui add button copies that component's source into your project. No package added to package.json, no version to track — the code is yours to edit.
ui.ad.why.point2.title: Or install the package and still ship only what you use
ui.ad.why.point2.body: pnpm add orn-ui is side-effect free and exports per subpath, so importing Button pulls in Button. Components you never import never reach your bundle.
ui.ad.why.point3.title: Setup is a single wrapper
ui.ad.why.point3.body: Wrap your app in UIProvider and every component has theme, icons, insets and labels. That is the entire configuration step.
ui.ad.why.closing: The point is speed: laying out real screens without rebuilding a Button for the fifth time, and without spending an agent's context writing primitives from scratch that already exist, tested, in the layer below.
ui.ad.what.title: The three layers
ui.ad.what.body: Brad Frost's original model has five levels — atoms, molecules, organisms, templates and pages. A component library can only own the first three: templates and pages describe your product, not a reusable package. So orn-ui stops at organisms and the last two layers stay in your app.
ui.ad.layers.atoms.def: The smallest useful piece. No composition, no business logic — it renders what it is given and reports back what the user did.
ui.ad.layers.atoms.rule: Split it and you are left with nothing usable.
ui.ad.layers.molecules.def: A few atoms wired together for one concrete job. It may hold local UI state, but it never knows where the data came from.
ui.ad.layers.molecules.rule: One job, describable in a short sentence without the word “and”.
ui.ad.layers.organisms.def: A self-contained section of a screen. Composes molecules and atoms, owns the interaction flow, and is the first layer allowed to touch data or navigation.
ui.ad.layers.organisms.rule: Drop it on an empty screen and it still makes sense on its own.
ui.ad.layers.direction: Dependencies only ever point downwards: organisms may import molecules and atoms, molecules may import atoms, atoms import nothing from the layers above. Break that direction once and the layers stop meaning anything.
ui.ad.benefits.title: Why bother
ui.ad.benefits.1.title: Naming stops being a debate
ui.ad.benefits.1.body: A new component's home is decided by what it depends on, not by taste. That removes one of the most recurring review arguments in a growing codebase.
ui.ad.benefits.2.title: Duplication becomes visible
ui.ad.benefits.2.body: When every primitive lives in one folder, a second Button someone wrote inside a screen file is obvious at a glance instead of surviving for a year.
ui.ad.benefits.3.title: Refactors stay local
ui.ad.benefits.3.body: Because dependencies point one way, changing an organism can never break an atom. The blast radius of a change is bounded by the layer you touched.
ui.ad.benefits.4.title: It maps onto tree-shaking
ui.ad.benefits.4.body: One-way layers are exactly what a bundler needs to drop unused code. In orn-ui, importing an atom pulls in that atom and nothing else.
ui.ad.benefits.5.title: New people ship on day one
ui.ad.benefits.5.body: “It goes in molecules” is a complete answer. Someone who has never seen the repo can place a component correctly.
ui.ad.how.title: How to apply it in any project
ui.ad.how.body: None of this is React Native specific. The same three folders work in Next.js, Vue, SwiftUI or plain CSS modules.
ui.ad.how.1.title: Create the folders
ui.ad.how.1.body: Three directories under components/, plus wherever your routes already live. Templates and pages are your existing screens — do not invent a new home for them.
ui.ad.how.2.title: Write down the one rule
ui.ad.how.2.body: Imports point downwards only. Enforce it mechanically if you can: import/no-restricted-paths in ESLint, or dependency-cruiser, fails the build instead of making a reviewer notice.
ui.ad.how.3.title: Start from the screen, not from the theory
ui.ad.how.3.body: Do not design an atom catalogue up front. Build a real screen, then pull out what it repeats. Anything used in three places has earned promotion to a lower layer.
ui.ad.how.4.title: Let the layer decide who owns state
ui.ad.how.4.body: Atoms are stateless and prop-driven. Molecules may hold local UI state — open/closed, focused index. Data fetching, stores and navigation start at organisms, never below.
ui.ad.how.5.title: Keep templates dumb and pages smart
ui.ad.how.5.body: A template is layout with holes in it; a page fills those holes with real data. That split is what lets you preview any layout without a backend.
ui.ad.mistakes.title: Three ways it goes wrong
ui.ad.mistakes.1: Classifying by size instead of by dependency. A tiny component that reads from a store is an organism, however few lines it has.
ui.ad.mistakes.2: Over-atomising. Wrapping every Text in a bespoke atom produces a hundred one-line files nobody remembers. Promote on the third repetition, not the first.
ui.ad.mistakes.3: Folders without the rule. Three directories with imports flying in every direction are the old mess under new names — the direction of dependency is the whole methodology.
ui.ad.map.title: How orn-ui is laid out
ui.ad.map.body: {atoms} atoms, {molecules} molecules and {organisms} organisms, each on its own page with props, variants and a recording from the simulator. Every one of them installs on its own.
ui.ad.sources.title: Sources
ui.ad.sources.body: The methodology is Brad Frost's, published in 2013 and expanded into a book that reads free online. The rest are the tools mentioned above and orn-ui's own source, which is where the component counts on this page come from.
ui.ad.sources.1.note: The 2013 post that introduced the chemistry analogy and the five stages.
ui.ad.sources.2.note: The book's full definition of atoms, molecules, organisms, templates and pages.
ui.ad.sources.3.note: ESLint rule used to enforce the import direction between layers.
ui.ad.sources.4.note: Validates and visualises dependencies; the alternative way to fail the build on a wrong-direction import.
ui.ad.sources.5.note: The library itself; the layers described here are the folders it ships.
ui.ad.diagram.caption: Source: Uxcel

alert.desc: Interrupting to confirm or report something that cannot wait. A Toast is enough for the rest.
Beyond confirm/cancel: a list with its own labels and handlers.
Renders it inside the layout instead of over the screen — for docs and demos.
Imperative, from outside the component tree — a service module, an interceptor. Needs an `AlertProvider` mounted once near the root. `showConfirm` resolves `true`/`false`.

avatar.desc: Representing a person or entity: profile headers, list rows, comment threads.
A number in points (44 by default). Keep one size per context.
Override for the circle; useful to color-code by entity type.

avatar-header.desc: The header of a profile or a detail screen: avatar, title and one supporting line.
Initials when there is a name; the icon when there is not.

badge.desc: A short read-only status attached to something else. It never handles a press.
Manual override, for statuses your product defines and the five variants do not cover.

bottom-sheet.desc: Actions or secondary content over the current screen, without leaving it.
Controlled: it closes on the backdrop and on gesture, always through `onClose`.
With a title the header appears with its close button. `footerPlacement` decides where the footer lives: fixed, at the end of the scroll, or hidden while the keyboard is up.
`draggable={false}` for a sheet that only closes by button or backdrop. `maxHeight` as a 0-1 fraction of the screen, or in pixels.

button.desc: The main action of a screen — one per view. Submit, confirm, continue.
A supporting action next to a primary one, when both matter.
Low-emphasis actions: cancel, dismiss, or repeated actions in a list.
Reads as text, not as a control — inline navigation inside a paragraph or footer.
Deletes or actions that cannot be undone. Pair it with a confirmation.
`md` by default. `lg` for a full-width call to action, `sm` inside dense rows or cards.
Use `loading` while an async action runs, `disabled` when the action is not available yet.

card.desc: Grouping related content into a surface: a summary, a list item with several lines, a form block.
It brings padding, radius and elevation, nothing else — the content inside is entirely yours.
Adjust spacing or width here rather than wrapping the Card in another View.

checkbox.desc: A binary choice that stands on its own: accept terms, remember me, toggle a filter.
Always controlled — the parent owns the state.
Tappable along with the box. Skip it only when a nearby text already labels it.
Accent override for the checked state; by default it follows the theme primary.

date-field.desc: A date inside a form: it reads like an Input and opens the calendar in a modal.
How the chosen date reads in the field. Match your locale.
Same pattern as Input and Select.
The strings of the modal, for when the app is not in English.

date-picker.desc: An inline calendar. To pick a date from a form, DateField wraps this one in a field.
`single` picks one date; `range` picks an interval with two taps.
Bound the selection instead of validating afterwards.
Localization: the component ships no translations of its own.
`0` Sunday, `1` Monday — a regional decision, not a stylistic one.

divider.desc: Separating sections of a list or a form when whitespace alone is not enough.
Change the margin here. Two dividers in a row, or one right after a section title, are usually noise.

empty-state.desc: A list or a search that returned nothing. Not for errors — those are Alert or a retry state.
The title names what is missing; the description says what to do about it.
`search` by default. Change it so the icon matches what is empty.

fab.desc: The single primary action of a screen, floating above the content. One per screen.
Offsets in points. Raise `bottom` when a tab bar or a footer sits underneath.
Required: the button is only an icon.

form-actions.desc: The action bar at the bottom of a form or a modal — keeps the order and spacing consistent.
If omitted, only the secondary button renders (a Cancel-only footer).
`primaryLoading` while the submit runs, `primaryDisabled` while the form is invalid.

icon-button.desc: An action with no room for a label — modal headers, list rows, toolbars. If the label fits, use Button.
`iconName` picks a bundled glyph; `icon` takes any node when the set falls short.
A number in points (24 by default). Keep it consistent within a row or header.
Required, and for good reason: there is no visible text, so it is the only thing a screen reader announces.

image.desc: Remote images that need a loading and an error state — which is most of them.
Same pattern as Avatar/Card. Set it here, not with an overflow wrapper.
What to show while it loads and if it fails. Both accept a node, so an image-shaped skeleton is fine.
`high` prefetches on mount — for the above-the-fold image of a screen, not for every item in a list.

info-row.desc: Read-only detail rows with an icon: contact data, order metadata.
Required, because a missing value is the common case — it makes the gap explicit instead of leaving a blank.

input.desc: `required` only paints the asterisk — validation stays with you.
Passing a string switches the field to its error state and shows the message below it.
Adds the show/hide toggle. Do not combine it with a right icon of your own.
The clearable, search or unit-toggle patterns: an icon of your choice plus its handler.
For fields that resolve something async (a lookup by code, a remote validation).

key-value-row.desc: Read-only pairs stacked in a column: totals, order details, a summary before confirming.
Takes a node, not only a string — a Badge or a bold amount works.
Emphasize the last row of a total without building a separate component.

list.desc: Any data list: it bundles loading, empty and pagination so each screen does not reinvent them.
`isLoading` is the data fetch; `isReady` is everything the screen needs before rendering at all.
Feed the EmptyState it renders when there is nothing to show.
Pagination: the callback loads, the flag shows the footer spinner.
`FlatList` by default; swap in FlashList without touching the rest.

modal.desc: `full` and `fullScreen` for a whole task; `overlay` for a short confirmation; `bottomSheet` for actions on the current context.
Also fires on the backdrop and the header X — keep it idempotent.
Where FormActions goes: it stays fixed while the content scrolls.
On by default. Turn it off when the content brings its own list.

navigation-bar.desc: The app's top-level sections, always visible. For a step flow inside one screen, Steps.
Controlled: the active tab lives in your navigator, not in the bar.
`bottom` by default; `top` for a segment-style bar under a header.

option-card.desc: Choosing between a few options, each with an icon — a payment method, a shipping type.
`horizontal` for a stacked list; `vertical` for a grid of two or three columns.
Controlled selection: the parent decides which one is on.

pressable-scale.desc: Giving press feedback to something that is not a Button: a card, a tile, a row.
`0.96` by default — noticeable without being distracting. Lower values suit small targets.
Also accepts a render prop that receives whether it is pressed, to restyle the content while held.

screen.desc: The root of every screen: it applies safe area, scroll and keyboard handling in one place.
`['top','bottom']` by default. Drop `bottom` when a tab bar already covers it.
Off when the content is a list — nesting a list inside a scroll breaks virtualization.
Off when the content already handles the keyboard (List, SearchList, Wizard): the two offsets add up.

search-list.desc: A list whose main entry point is a search field. Otherwise, List.
Controlled: debounce and query live in your screen, not in the component.
`replace` swaps the list for a spinner; `overlay` keeps the layout, which avoids the jump while typing.
Adds the scan action next to the field — for codes, QR, barcodes.
Pagination with an explicit end, so the footer says when there is nothing left.

segmented-control.desc: A few options, all visible at once, one always selected — a view or range switch. For a longer or optional list, Select.
Controlled and generic, same pattern as Select — the value keeps its type.
Per-option or for the whole control.

select.desc: Picking one option from a closed list. For two or three options with an icon, OptionCard reads better.
Controlled and generic: the value keeps its type, it is not forced into a string.
Same pattern as Input, so a form mixing both stays consistent.
For options that arrive from the network.

skeleton.desc: A placeholder that reserves the exact space of content still loading. For a spinner without that shape, Spinner.
Only for `variant="text"`: a stacked paragraph whose last line is shorter, so it doesn't read as a solid block.
Set it to false to respect reduced motion or to save cycles in a long list.

spinner.desc: `native` is the system indicator and the right default. `dots` and `ring` look identical on iOS and Android when that matters.
`true` takes the whole area; set it to `false` for an inline spinner inside a row or a card.
A short line under the indicator. Use it when the wait is long enough to need explaining.
Your own node, when the brand asks for something the three variants do not cover.

stepper.desc: Small numeric amounts adjusted by hand: quantities, units, servings.
The value is a string: the field stays editable and empty states do not turn into NaN.
`md` by default, `sm` inside dense rows such as a cart line.

steps.desc: Showing progress through a known sequence. It only displays state — Wizard is the one that navigates.
`horizontal` for three or four short steps; `vertical` when the labels are long.
A check by default; `number` when the step number is what people refer to.
Makes each step tappable. Only wire it if going back is actually allowed.

theme-toggle.desc: Letting the user pick light, dark or system — usually in settings.
Override the three built-in strings when your product words them differently.

toast.desc: Confirming something that already happened, without interrupting. If a decision is needed, it is an Alert.
`success`, `error`, `warning`, `info` — the same semantics as Badge and Alert.
Makes it tappable: usually to open what it is talking about. It also dismisses.
Hides the X. It still auto-dismisses on a timer.
Imperative, from outside the component tree — a service module, an interceptor. Needs a `ToastProvider` mounted once near the root. Returns the id for `hideToast(id)`.

transition.desc: Mounting/unmounting a node with a native-thread animation instead of a hard cut. Modal, BottomSheet and Toast already use it internally.
One or an array — `['fade', 'slide-up']` combines opacity and a slide. `pop` is a spring by default.
One index per item staggers a list — no need for a separate library.
Hands progress (0→1) to an outside driver, e.g. a PanResponder, instead of a timing/spring.

wizard.desc: A multi-step flow with navigation. To only show progress, Steps is enough.
Optional: without them the Wizard keeps its own state, which covers most flows.
Per-step validation — the step declares whether it lets you move on.
Lets people jump back to a completed step from the indicator.
Off only if a step renders its own virtualized list.

propDescriptions.AvatarHeader.iconName: Icon shown inside the circle. If omitted, `initials` are used.
propDescriptions.AvatarHeader.initials: Short text (e.g. 2 letters) shown when `iconName` is not passed.
propDescriptions.DateField.format: Formats the date shown in the field.
propDescriptions.DatePicker.defaultMonth: Month shown on open when there is no `value`.
propDescriptions.DatePicker.mode: 'single' picks one date; 'range' picks an interval with two taps.
propDescriptions.DatePicker.onRangeChange: Called in mode="range", both when setting the start and when closing the range.
propDescriptions.FormActions.primaryLabel: If omitted, only the secondary button is shown.
propDescriptions.Image.fallback: What to show if loading fails.
propDescriptions.Image.loading: What to show while loading. `false` shows nothing.
propDescriptions.Image.priority:
'high' fires Image.prefetch() on mount, before <Image> starts its own
loading cycle — meant for the above-the-fold image of a screen (the first
one the user sees). Free if it is already cached.
propDescriptions.Image.radius: Corner radius, same pattern as Avatar/Card.
propDescriptions.Input.required: Shows an asterisk next to the label. Purely visual — it does not validate anything.
propDescriptions.List.isReady: Controlled by the consumer: while false, a full-screen spinner is shown.
propDescriptions.NavigationBar.position: Edge of the screen the bar lives on.
propDescriptions.NavigationBar.safeArea: Adds the safe area inset of the edge the bar lives on.
propDescriptions.OptionCard.layout: 'vertical': icon on top, text centered below. 'horizontal': icon and text in a row.
propDescriptions.Screen.edges: Which safe area insets to apply.
propDescriptions.Screen.keyboardAvoiding:
Offsets the keyboard with a KeyboardAvoidingView. Set it to false when the
content already brings its own scroller that handles the keyboard (Wizard,
List, SearchList): both offsets add up and the focused field ends up pushed
off screen.
propDescriptions.SearchList.header: Optional chrome above the search field (e.g. back button + title).
propDescriptions.SearchList.loadingMode: 'replace' swaps the whole list for a spinner; 'overlay' shows it on top, keeping the layout.
propDescriptions.Skeleton.lastLineWidth: Width of the last line, so the paragraph doesn't end in a solid block.
propDescriptions.Spinner.variant:
'native' uses the system ActivityIndicator; 'dots' and 'ring' are custom
indicators, identical on iOS and Android.
propDescriptions.Steps.completedIndicator: What the circle of a completed step shows: a check, or its number.
propDescriptions.Steps.current: Index of the current step (0-based). Earlier ones are marked 'completed'.
propDescriptions.Steps.onStepPress: If passed, every step becomes tappable and reports its index.
propDescriptions.Toast.hideCloseButton: Hides the close X. The toast still auto-dismisses on a timer.
propDescriptions.Toast.onPress: Fires when the toast is tapped (on top of dismissing it).
propDescriptions.Transition.appear: Also animates the first render. On false it starts already present.
propDescriptions.Transition.delay: ms before starting. One delay per index staggers a list.
propDescriptions.Transition.keepMounted: Keeps the node mounted on exit, only hides it.
propDescriptions.Transition.preset: One or several: `['fade', 'scale']` combines opacity and scale.
propDescriptions.Transition.value:
Progress 0→1 driven from outside. With this, Transition only interpolates:
whoever passes it decides when and how it advances (a PanResponder, for example).
propDescriptions.Transition.visible: Mounts on true, exits (and unmounts) on false.
propDescriptions.Wizard.allowStepNavigation: Allows going back to an already completed step by tapping it in the indicator.
propDescriptions.Wizard.current: Current step (controlled). If omitted, the Wizard keeps its own state.
propDescriptions.Wizard.scrollableContent:
The step content scrolls when it does not fit. Set it to false only if a step
renders its own virtualized list (nesting a VirtualizedList inside a
ScrollView breaks virtualization).

propDefaults.DateField.format: "D de Month de YYYY" in English
propDefaults.Image.fallback: a plain grey placeholder, no content
